title: Class-wise Balancing Data Replay for Federated Class-Incremental Learning

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Table 1 states that CIFAR10 heterogeneity settings are 0.5/1.0, but Tables 2 and 3 report results for CIFAR10 with β=0.1 (a third heterogeneity level not listed in Table 1).

The caption says 'Comparison of per-class sample distributions in the replay buffer ...', but the figure shows line plots of test accuracy vs. task ID (performance over incremental tasks), not sample distributions.

The text cites references [59]-[63] to support Grad-CAM visualizations. These references are about federated learning, causal inference, and multimodal retrieval, not about Grad-CAM. The original Grad-CAM work (Selvaraju et al.) is not cited.

Table 3 includes a column for TinyImageNet β=0.1 but contains no entries for any method, while Table 2 (with a different task split) contains values for the same heterogeneity level. This missing data is unexplained and makes the table inconsistent.

The GDR module encrypts local features using client-specific random orthogonal matrices P_k before aggregation and SVD, claiming to enable exploration of global distribution. Because each client's features are rotated by a different unknown orthogonal matrix, the concatenated matrix loses cross-client alignment; the resulting leverage scores from the SVD of this scrambled matrix do not reflect true global importance and cannot guide meaningful class-balanced sampling. This invalidates the claimed 'global-perspective' sampling.

The text states 'aggregates them into a global vector ... and normalizes it to obtain a sampling distribution: p_k^{i,j} = τ_k^{i,j} / ∑_{j'=1}^{n_k^i} τ_k^{i,j'}'. This normalizes per client rather than across all clients, contradicting the claim of global aggregation. The resulting sampling remains per-client, not globally balanced.

Section 4.2 defines the TTS loss as a weighted sum of cross-entropies computed separately on old-class and new-class logits (Eq. 7). Section 4.3 instead defines the loss using the concatenation of temperature-scaled old and new logits for each sample (Eq. 9). These two formulations are structurally different and cannot both be the correct loss used in the method.
